107058.q: Which seasoning can raise blood pressure if you eat a lot of it?
107058.e: Lots of table salt holds water in the body and can make blood pressure rise in many people. Ready meals often contain lots of hidden salt.
107058.m: Too much salt can push blood pressure up.

107059.q: Which brain condition becomes more likely after years of high blood pressure?
107059.e: Over time, high pressure damages the walls of the blood vessels. This increases the risk that a vessel in the brain becomes blocked or bursts.
107059.m: Untreated high blood pressure increases the risk of a stroke.

107060.q: What helps most to prevent high blood pressure?
107060.e: Regular exercise strengthens the heart and blood vessels and helps keep a healthy weight. Both lower the risk of high blood pressure.
107060.m: Regular exercise protects your blood vessels.

107061.q: What is the opposite of high blood pressure, meaning blood pressure that is too low, called?
107061.e: The prefix “hypo” means under or too little. That is why blood pressure that is low all the time is called hypotension.
107061.m: Blood pressure that is too low is called hypotension.

107062.q: Which organs that filter the blood can high blood pressure damage?
107062.e: The kidneys contain many fine vessels that filter the blood. Constant high pressure can damage these vessels and make the kidneys work less well.
107062.m: High blood pressure can damage the kidneys.

107063.q: Which drink raises blood pressure if you regularly drink a lot of it?
107063.e: Regularly drinking a lot of alcohol is one of the known causes of high blood pressure. Drinking less alcohol can lower blood pressure again.
107063.m: Lots of alcohol can raise blood pressure for good.

107064.q: What is the technical term for a short faint?
107064.e: A syncope is a short loss of consciousness from which you quickly recover. The term comes from Greek.
107064.m: A short faint is called a syncope.

a: The brain briefly gets too little blood
107065.e: In a faint, the brain briefly gets too little blood. As a result it lacks oxygen and you lose consciousness for a short time.
107065.m: In a faint, the brain briefly gets too little blood.

107066.q: How do you help a person who has briefly fainted and is breathing normally?
a: Lay them flat and raise their legs
Stand them up at once and make them walk
Give them cold water to drink
107066.e: If the legs are raised, more blood flows to the heart and brain. The person then usually comes round quickly.
107066.m: When someone faints, raise their legs.

107067.q: How long does an ordinary faint usually last?
a: Only seconds to a few minutes
107067.e: With a syncope, you quickly come round by yourself, usually after seconds. If the unconsciousness lasts longer, medical help is needed.
107067.m: An ordinary faint is over after a short time.

107068.q: Which situation can trigger a faint especially easily?
a: Standing for a long time in great heat
107068.e: When you stand for a long time in the heat, the blood vessels widen and blood collects in the legs. The brain then lacks blood.
107068.m: Standing for a long time in the heat can lead to fainting.

107069.q: Which warning sign often comes before a faint?
a: Everything goes black before your eyes
107069.e: Before a faint, dizziness, blackouts in your vision and nausea often occur. If you notice this, it is best to sit or lie down straight away.
107069.m: If everything goes black before your eyes, sit down straight away.

107070.q: A person stays unconscious but is breathing normally. How do you position them?
a: On their front with the face down
107070.e: In the recovery position, the airways stay clear and vomit can drain away. Then you call for help and keep checking the breathing.
107070.m: Unconscious people who breathe normally go into the recovery position.

107071.q: Why do some people briefly faint at the sight of blood?
a: A nerve reaction suddenly lowers pulse and blood pressure
The blood evaporates and makes you tired
The eyes are dazzled by the red
The stomach pulls all the blood towards it
107071.e: In this so-called vasovagal syncope, the nervous system overreacts. Heartbeat and blood pressure drop briefly, and the brain gets too little blood.
107071.m: A fright or the sight of blood can trigger a faint through the nerves.

107072.q: What happens in a circulatory collapse?
107072.e: In a circulatory collapse, blood pressure suddenly drops. The brain gets less blood, you feel weak and can collapse.
107072.m: A circulatory collapse is a sudden drop in blood pressure.

107073.q: Which movement makes some people dizzy because their blood pressure drops?
a: Getting up too quickly from lying down
Breathing out deeply while lying down
107073.e: When you get up quickly, blood flows into the legs before the circulation has adjusted. For a moment, the brain gets too little blood.
107073.m: If you get up quickly, your blood pressure can drop for a moment.

107074.q: When you stand still for a long time, where does a lot of blood pool?
107074.e: Because of gravity, blood collects in the veins of the legs. Without muscle movement, it only flows back to the heart slowly.
107074.m: When you stand for a long time, blood collects in the legs.

107075.q: What helps prevent a circulatory collapse on hot days?
a: Standing in the sun for a long time
107075.e: In the heat, the body loses a lot of fluid through sweating. If the blood is short of fluid, blood pressure drops more easily.
107075.m: Drinking enough in the heat protects your circulation.

107076.q: What helps against a circulatory collapse when standing for a long time?
a: Moving your toes and calves again and again
Holding your breath as long as possible
Holding your arms high above your head
107076.e: Working calf muscles squeeze the veins and push the blood towards the heart. This muscle pump keeps the circulation going.
107076.m: Moving calf muscles pump the blood back from the legs.

107077.q: What is a circulatory collapse caused by great heat called?
107077.e: In great heat, the blood vessels in the skin widen to give off warmth. This can make blood pressure drop so much that a heat collapse happens.
107077.m: Great heat can cause a heat collapse.

107078.q: What does the skin often look like during a circulatory collapse?
107078.e: In a collapse, the blood vessels in the skin narrow and a cold sweat breaks out. That is why the person looks pale.
107078.m: In a circulatory collapse, the skin is often pale and damp.

107079.q: What should you be careful about when getting up after a circulatory collapse?
a: Sit up slowly and only then stand up
Jump up at once and run
107079.e: The circulation needs time to recover. If you get up too quickly, you risk collapsing again.
107079.m: After a collapse, get up again only slowly.

a: Hardening and narrowing of the arteries
107080.e: In arteriosclerosis, substances build up in the artery wall. The artery becomes hard, narrow and less elastic.
107080.m: Arteriosclerosis makes the arteries hard and narrow.

107081.q: What is arteriosclerosis often called in everyday language?
107081.e: Because the deposits also contain lime (calcium), people often call it hardening of the arteries. The medical term is arteriosclerosis.
107081.m: In everyday language, arteriosclerosis is called hardening of the arteries.

107082.q: What are the deposits in the artery walls called?
107082.e: The deposits in the vessel wall are called plaques. They are made of fat, connective tissue and lime, among other things.
107082.m: The deposits in arteriosclerosis are called plaques.

107083.q: Which blood fat plays an important part in arteriosclerosis?
107083.e: Too much LDL cholesterol in the blood encourages plaques to form. That is why cholesterol levels are often measured at check-ups.
107083.m: Too much cholesterol in the blood encourages hardening of the arteries.

107084.q: Which habit is one of the strongest risk factors for arteriosclerosis?
107084.e: The substances in tobacco smoke damage the inner wall of the blood vessels. Deposits form more easily at the damaged spots.
107084.m: Smoking damages the blood vessels and encourages arteriosclerosis.

107085.q: What can happen if a coronary artery is blocked by arteriosclerosis?
107085.e: If a coronary artery is blocked, part of the heart muscle no longer gets any oxygen. This part dies if help does not come quickly.
107085.m: A blocked coronary artery causes a heart attack.

107086.q: What is the circulation problem in the legs called, in which people often have to stop and stand still?
107086.e: Narrowed leg arteries cause pain when walking that eases at rest. People with it often stop as if they were looking in shop windows, which is why it is also nicknamed “window-shopper’s disease”.
107086.m: Narrowed leg arteries cause intermittent claudication.

107087.q: How quickly does arteriosclerosis normally develop?
107087.e: The deposits grow slowly over years and decades. That is why a healthy lifestyle is worthwhile even when you are young.
107087.m: Arteriosclerosis develops gradually over many years.

a: A blood clot blocks a blood vessel
107088.e: In a thrombosis, a clot forms in a blood vessel. It can partly or completely block the vessel.
107088.m: In a thrombosis, a blood clot blocks a vessel.

107089.q: What is the blood clot that forms in a thrombosis called?
107089.e: The clot is called a thrombus. It is mainly made of blood platelets, fibrin and trapped blood cells.
107089.m: A blood clot in a vessel is called a thrombus.

107090.q: Where do thromboses form most often?
a: In the deep veins of the legs
In the tip of the nose
107090.e: In the deep veins of the legs, blood flows slowly against gravity. Clots form there most often.
107090.m: Thromboses usually form in the deep veins of the legs.

107091.q: Which dangerous consequence can a thrombosis in a leg vein have?
107091.e: If a clot comes loose, it can be carried with the blood through the heart into the lungs. There it blocks a vessel, which can be life-threatening.
107091.m: A clot that comes loose can cause a pulmonary embolism.

107092.q: Which situation increases the risk of a thrombosis?
a: Sitting for hours on a long-haul flight
107092.e: When you sit for a long time, the calf muscles hardly work and the blood flows slowly. That is why you should get up and move your legs on long journeys.
107092.m: Sitting for a long time without moving increases the risk of thrombosis.

107093.q: Which stockings are worn to prevent a thrombosis?
107093.e: Compression stockings put pressure on the legs. This makes the blood in the veins flow back to the heart faster.

107094.q: Which medicines are used to treat a thrombosis?
107094.e: Anticoagulants, often called blood thinners, stop the clot from growing. Then the body can slowly break it down.
107094.m: Anticoagulants stop a blood clot from growing.

107095.q: How can you often recognise a thrombosis in a leg vein?
a: The leg is swollen, warm and painful
The leg only itches on the sole
The leg feels ice cold and numb
107095.e: When blood backs up behind the clot, the leg swells. It often feels warm and tight and hurts.
107095.m: A swollen, warm and painful leg can be a sign of thrombosis.

a: A pale fluid in the lymph vessels
A hormone from the thyroid gland
107096.e: Lymph is a clear to yellowish fluid. It flows through the body in its own system of vessels.
107096.m: Lymph is a pale body fluid.

107097.e: A little fluid constantly leaks out of the capillaries into the tissue. Some of it is taken up by lymph vessels and is then called lymph.
107097.m: Lymph forms from the fluid between the cells.

107098.q: Where does lymph flow in the end?
a: Into the blood in the veins near the heart
107098.e: The large lymph ducts open into large veins near the heart. In this way the fluid returns to the bloodstream.
107098.m: Lymph flows back into the blood near the heart.

107099.q: What job do the lymph nodes have?
a: They filter the lymph and fight germs
They pump blood around the body
They store lime for the bones
107099.e: Lymph nodes are filter stations in the lymphatic system. Germs are caught there and fought by defence cells.
107099.m: Lymph nodes are filter stations of the body’s defences.

107100.q: Which white blood cells are found especially often in lymph?
107100.e: Lymphocytes are defence cells named after lymph. Erythrocytes are red blood cells and thrombocytes are blood platelets.
107100.m: Lymphocytes are defence cells that circulate in the lymph.

107101.q: What pushes lymph along the lymph vessels?
a: A lymph heart of its own in the chest
107101.e: The lymphatic system has no central pump like the heart. Muscle movements, breathing and valves in the lymph vessels push the lymph along.
107101.m: Muscle movements push lymph through the body.

107102.q: What is the largest lymph duct in the body called?
107102.e: The thoracic duct, in Latin ductus thoracicus, collects lymph from most of the body. It opens into the veins on the left side of the neck.
107102.m: The thoracic duct is the largest lymph duct.

107103.q: Why do the lymph nodes in the neck often swell when you have a sore throat?
a: Because they store water for the voice
107103.e: During an infection, defence cells multiply in the lymph nodes. This makes the nodes bigger and sometimes tender when pressed.
107103.m: Swollen lymph nodes show that the body is fighting germs.

107104.q: Which nutrients does lymph especially take up in the intestines?
107104.e: In the intestines, fats from food first pass into the lymph vessels. That is why the lymph there looks milky and cloudy.
107104.m: In the intestines, lymph mainly carries the fats taken up from food.

a: A build-up of water in the tissue
107105.e: With oedema, fluid collects in the tissue between the cells. The affected area swells up.
107105.m: Oedema is swelling caused by water in the tissue.

107106.q: Where does oedema appear especially often in many people?
a: On the ankles and lower legs
On the tip of the nose
107106.e: Because of gravity, fluid easily collects in the lower part of the legs. That is why the ankles often swell.
107106.m: Oedema often shows first on the ankles.

107107.q: How can you often recognise oedema on the skin?
a: Pressing with a finger leaves a dent
The skin glows in the dark
107107.e: If you press on the swollen area, the fluid is pushed away. The dent stays visible for a while.
107107.m: With oedema, a dent stays after pressing with a finger.

107108.q: Which heart condition often leads to oedema in the legs?
107108.e: If the heart pumps too weakly, the blood backs up in the veins. More fluid then leaks into the tissue of the legs.
107108.m: A weak heart can cause water to build up in the legs.

107109.q: Why is pulmonary oedema, water in the lungs, dangerous?
107109.e: In pulmonary oedema, fluid leaks into the air sacs of the lungs. Then there is no room for air, and the person struggles to breathe. It is an emergency.
107109.m: Pulmonary oedema is water in the lungs and a medical emergency.

107110.q: What is oedema called that is caused by lymph not draining properly?
107110.e: If lymph cannot drain properly, fluid builds up in the tissue. A special massage called lymphatic drainage can help.
107110.m: Blocked lymph drainage leads to lymphoedema.

107111.q: Why do feet often swell on hot summer days?
a: The vessels widen and fluid leaks out
The bones expand in the warmth
The muscles grow because of the heat
107111.e: Heat widens the blood vessels. As a result, more fluid leaks into the tissue, especially in the feet and ankles.
107111.m: Heat makes feet swell because the vessels widen.

107112.q: What are medicines that flush out oedema called?
107112.e: Water tablets, also called diuretics, make the kidneys get rid of more water and salt. This makes the build-up of water go down.
107112.m: Water tablets help the body get rid of stored water.

107213.q: What is the young, still closed fruiting body of the stinkhorn called, which looks like an egg?
107213.e: The stinkhorn first grows inside an egg-shaped, jelly-like casing. Later the stalk with the smelly head shoots out of it.
107213.m: The young fruiting body of the stinkhorn is called a witch's egg.

107214.q: What is the main job of a fungus's fruiting body?
107214.e: The spores the fungus uses to reproduce are formed in the fruiting body. The wind or animals carry them further.
107214.m: The fruiting body produces and spreads the spores.

107215.q: Which two main parts make up the fruiting body of a typical cap mushroom?
107215.e: A cap mushroom such as the cep has a stalk with a cap on top. The spores are formed on the underside of the cap.
107215.m: A cap mushroom consists of a cap and a stalk.

107216.q: Why can fungi not carry out photosynthesis?
107216.e: Fungi have no green chlorophyll. So they have to get their food from living or dead organisms.
107216.m: Fungi have no chlorophyll and cannot carry out photosynthesis.

107217.q: According to current knowledge, which group of living things do fungi belong to?
a: To a kingdom of their own
107217.e: Fungi used to be counted as plants. Today they form a kingdom of their own and are even more closely related to animals than to plants.
107217.m: Fungi form a kingdom of their own alongside plants and animals.

107218.q: Which white, round fungus can form a fruiting body as big as a football?
107218.e: The giant puffball forms round, white fruiting bodies usually 10 to 50 centimetres across. Countless spores ripen inside.
107218.m: The giant puffball can grow as big as a football.

107219.q: What is the technical term for the ring on the stalk of some mushrooms, for example the fly agaric?
107219.e: The ring is what is left of a skin that covered the underside of the cap in the young mushroom. It is called the annulus.
107219.m: The ring on a mushroom's stalk is called the annulus.

107220.q: Why is the death cap particularly dangerous?
a: It is deadly poisonous and easily confused
107220.e: Even a single death cap can be deadly. Young ones are easily confused with edible species. That is why gathered mushrooms are taken to a mushroom inspection office.
107220.m: The death cap is deadly poisonous.

107221.q: When do most mushroom fruiting bodies grow in Switzerland?
a: Only in dry weather in July
107221.e: Fungi need warmth and a lot of moisture. These conditions are usually found in late summer and autumn.
107221.m: The main mushroom season is late summer and autumn.

107222.e: Fungi are made of microscopically thin threads called hyphae. They grow at their tips and run through the soil.
107222.m: Hyphae are the fine threads a fungus is made of.

107223.q: Where do fungal hyphae grow longer?
a: At their end in the cap
107223.e: Hyphae get longer at their very tip. That way they can work their way purposefully through soil or wood.

107224.q: What is the underground network of fungal threads, through which trees exchange substances, jokingly called?
107224.e: Fungal hyphae can connect the roots of several trees. Based on the internet, people therefore speak of the “Wood Wide Web”.
107224.m: Fungal threads connect trees like an underground network.

107225.q: Some fungi live together with the roots of a tree (mycorrhiza). What does the fungus get from the tree?
107225.e: The tree makes sugar through photosynthesis. It passes some of it to the fungus through its roots.
107225.m: In mycorrhiza, the fungus gets sugar from the tree.

107226.q: Some fungi live together with the roots of a tree (mycorrhiza). What do the fungal threads supply to the tree?
107226.e: The fine network of fungal threads reaches much further into the soil than the tree's roots. That way it can carry water and minerals to the tree.
107226.m: Fungal hyphae supply trees with water and mineral nutrients.

107227.q: How do fungal hyphae take in their food?
a: They release digestive substances and absorb dissolved matter
They eat small animals through a tiny mouth
They make their own sugar using sunlight
They take in only pure rainwater from the soil
107227.e: Hyphae release enzymes that break down food outside the fungus. They then absorb the dissolved building blocks through their surface.
107227.m: Fungi digest their food outside their body.

107228.q: What are fungi called that attack living trees with their hyphae and harm them?
107228.e: Parasitic fungi take nutrients from their host and weaken it. Honey fungus, for example, can kill whole trees.
107228.m: Fungi that harm living trees are parasites.

107229.q: Why can a single fungus be one of the largest living things on Earth?
a: Its network of threads in the soil is huge
Its cap is as big as a house
It grows up into the clouds
It floats as a carpet in the sea
107229.e: Most of a fungus is the network of fungal threads in the soil. In one honey fungus in the USA, it stretches over several square kilometres.
107229.m: The network of threads of a fungus can become huge.

107230.q: How can you recognise a bolete (a mushroom with tubes)?
a: By the sponge-like underside of the cap made of tubes
By the thin gills under the cap
By having no stalk and a round body
By the honeycomb-like cap surface with pits
107230.e: In boletes, the underside of the cap consists of many tightly packed tubes. From below it looks like a sponge.
107230.m: Boletes have a sponge-like layer of tubes under the cap.

107231.q: What are the small openings of the tubes on the underside of the cap called?
107231.e: Each tube ends at the bottom with a small opening, the pore. The spores fall out through it.
107231.m: The openings of the tubes are called pores.

107232.q: Which popular edible mushroom is a bolete?
107232.e: The cep has a layer of tubes under its brown cap, which is white at first and later yellowish green. It belongs to the boletes.

107233.q: Which bolete looks like the cep but is so bitter that it ruins a whole dish?
107233.e: The bitter bolete is not poisonous, but extremely bitter. Its tubes turn pink with age, while those of the cep turn yellowish green.
107233.m: The bitter bolete is a lookalike of the cep.

107234.q: What happens with many boletes when you press on the tubes?
107234.e: Many boletes, such as the bay bolete, turn blue when pressed. This is a chemical reaction with oxygen in the air.
107234.m: Many boletes turn blue when pressed.

107235.q: Near which conifer, which loses its needles in autumn, does the larch bolete grow?
107235.e: The larch bolete gets its name because it lives only with larches. Fungus and tree exchange water and sugar through the roots.
107235.m: The larch bolete grows near larches.

107236.q: Where are the spores formed in a bolete?
a: On the inner walls of the tubes
On the top of the cap
In the bulb at the base of the stalk
107236.e: The insides of the tubes are lined with spore-forming tissue. The ripe spores trickle out at the bottom.
107236.m: Boletes form their spores in the tubes.

107237.q: Which bolete with a red stalk and an unpleasant smell is poisonous?
107237.e: The devil's bolete has a pale cap, red pores and a stalk with a red net pattern. It causes severe stomach and bowel problems.
107237.m: The devil's bolete is a poisonous bolete.

107238.q: Why should you show mushrooms you have picked yourself to a mushroom inspection office before eating them?
a: Many poisonous mushrooms look very like edible ones
Because otherwise you are not allowed to cook mushrooms
So that the mushrooms are weighed
107238.e: Among the gilled mushrooms there are deadly poisonous species that are easily confused. In many Swiss municipalities, experts check mushrooms for free.
107238.m: Always have mushrooms checked at a mushroom inspection office.

107239.q: What advantage do gills give a mushroom?
a: They increase the area for forming spores
107239.e: With its many thin plates, the mushroom has a very large surface. On it, it can form a particularly large number of spores.
107239.m: Gills increase the surface for the spores.

107240.q: Which gilled mushroom grows sideways on wood like a shell and is often cultivated too?
107240.e: The oyster mushroom grows in overlapping layers on broadleaved wood. It is easy to grow on straw or wood and is sold in shops.
107240.m: The oyster mushroom grows on wood like a shell.

107241.q: Why is identifying gilled mushrooms particularly tricky for beginners?
a: They include many deadly poisonous species
They are all the same colour
107241.e: The most dangerous poisonous mushrooms in Central Europe, such as the death caps, are gilled mushrooms. Among the boletes there are hardly any deadly poisonous species in Central Europe.
107241.m: Among the gilled mushrooms there are many deadly poisonous species.

107242.q: What happens to a shaggy ink cap when it gets old?
a: It dissolves into a black liquid
It becomes rock hard like wood
107242.e: The gills of the shaggy ink cap turn black with age and dissolve. People even used to make ink from the black liquid.
107242.m: With age, the shaggy ink cap dissolves into black ink.

107243.q: How can you recognise a gilled mushroom?
a: Lots of thin plates sit under the cap
Under the cap there is a sponge of tubes
The mushroom has no cap at all
107243.e: Gills are thin plates on the underside of the cap. Boletes such as the cep have a sponge-like cushion of tubes there instead.
107243.m: Gilled mushrooms have thin plates under the cap.

107244.q: Which large gilled mushroom has a movable ring on its stalk and a cap like an umbrella?
107244.e: The parasol mushroom can form a cap over 20 centimetres across. Its double ring can be slid up and down the stalk.
107244.m: The parasol mushroom has a movable ring on its stalk.

107245.q: Which group of fungi do brittlegills belong to?
107245.e: Brittlegills have brittle gills that break easily and an often colourful cap. Their flesh breaks like chalk.
107245.m: Brittlegills are gilled mushrooms with brittle flesh.

107246.q: Why should you throw away a whole loaf of bread with a small spot of mould?
a: The invisible fungal network can run through the whole loaf
The spot makes the whole loaf rock hard at once
Mould is only harmful on the surface
The bread then tastes far too sweet
107246.e: What you see are only the spore carriers. The fine fungal threads and their toxins can spread invisibly through the soft bread.
107246.m: Mouldy bread belongs entirely in the bin.

107247.q: Which important medicine was obtained from a mould?
107247.e: In 1928, Alexander Fleming discovered that a mould kills bacteria. This led to penicillin, the first antibiotic.

107248.q: Which mould gives Roquefort cheese its blue-green veins?
107248.e: The noble mould Penicillium roqueforti grows in the holes of the cheese. It gives blue cheese its colour and flavour.
107248.m: Noble mould turns blue cheese like Roquefort blue.

107249.q: Which cheese has a white rind made of noble mould?
107249.e: Camembert and Brie are covered with a white noble mould. It forms the fluffy rind and makes the cheese soft.
107249.m: Camembert has a white rind made of noble mould.

107250.q: What helps best against mould on the walls of a flat?
a: Putting furniture right up against the outside wall
107250.e: Mould needs moisture. Airing in short bursts and heating let damp air escape outside, and the walls stay dry.
107250.m: Regular airing helps against mould in a flat.

107251.q: Which mould often attacks strawberries and grapes with a grey fur?
107251.e: Grey mould, Botrytis cinerea, grows on fruit in damp weather. On grapes, under certain conditions, it can be welcome as noble rot.
107251.m: Grey mould covers strawberries with a grey fur.

107252.q: Why should you not eat nuts that smell musty or taste bitter?
107252.e: On spoilt nuts, moulds can form very dangerous toxins. They are called aflatoxins and are not destroyed by roasting.
107252.m: Spoilt nuts may contain poisonous mould.

107253.e: Moulds produce huge amounts of tiny spores. These float in the air almost everywhere and sprout wherever it is damp and there is food.
107253.m: Mould spores are in the air almost everywhere.

107254.e: Baker's yeast consists of tiny single-celled fungi. One block of yeast contains billions of these cells.
107254.m: Baker's yeast consists of single-celled fungi.

107255.q: What does baker's yeast feed on in dough?
107255.e: Yeast uses sugar from the flour. This produces carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise.

107256.q: What is the process called in which yeast turns sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide without oxygen?
107256.e: In alcoholic fermentation, yeast gets energy from sugar. This produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

107257.q: How do yeast cells usually reproduce?
a: A daughter cell grows out of the mother cell
107257.e: A small daughter cell grows out of the mother cell and breaks off once it is big enough. This is called budding.
107257.m: Yeast cells reproduce by daughter cells growing out of them.

107258.q: Why should you not mix fresh yeast with boiling hot water?
107258.e: Yeast works best at lukewarm temperatures of about 30 degrees. Too much heat kills the cells, and the dough no longer rises.
107258.m: Yeast needs lukewarm liquid, not boiling.

107259.q: What happens to the alcohol that yeast produces in bread dough?
107259.e: Yeast produces only a little alcohol in the dough. At the high temperatures in the oven, it evaporates.
107259.m: The alcohol from yeast dough evaporates during baking.

107260.q: Apart from baking bread, which drink is yeast also used for?
107260.e: When beer is brewed, yeast ferments the malt sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Wine is also made by yeast fermentation.
107260.m: Yeast is also used for brewing beer.

107261.q: Why do scientists like to do research with baker's yeast?
a: It is easy to grow and multiplies quickly
It is as big as an egg
It lives only in the sea
It is very rare and expensive
107261.e: Baker's yeast is an important model in research. In 1996, its genome was the first of any organism with a cell nucleus to be fully decoded.
107261.m: Baker's yeast is an important subject of research.

107262.e: The Scottish bacteriologist Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould on a bacterial culture killed the bacteria. That is how he discovered penicillin.

107263.q: What is the mould called from which penicillin is obtained?
107263.e: Penicillin comes from the mould Penicillium, from the Latin for “little brush”. Under the microscope, its spore carriers look like tiny brushes.
107263.m: Penicillin comes from the mould Penicillium.

107264.q: During which war was penicillin first produced in large amounts?
107264.e: From about 1943, penicillin was produced in large amounts in the USA and Great Britain. It saved the lives of many wounded soldiers.
107264.m: Penicillin was first mass-produced in the Second World War.

107265.q: Which germs does penicillin work against?
107265.e: Penicillin kills certain bacteria or stops them growing. It does not work against viruses, for example in flu.
107265.m: Penicillin works against bacteria, not viruses.

107266.q: Which group of medicines does penicillin belong to?
107266.e: Antibiotics are substances that kill bacteria or stop them growing. Penicillin was the first antibiotic to be widely used.

a: It disrupts the building of their cell wall
107267.e: Penicillin stops growing bacteria from building their cell wall. Without a stable wall, the bacteria burst.
107267.m: Penicillin disrupts the bacteria's cell wall building.

107268.q: Which award did Fleming, Florey and Chain receive in 1945 for penicillin?
107268.e: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain made penicillin usable as a medicine. Together with Fleming, they received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945.
107268.m: Penicillin won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1945.

107269.q: What does it mean when bacteria are resistant to an antibiotic?
a: The medicine no longer works against them
107269.e: Using antibiotics too often or wrongly can let insensitive bacteria win out. The medicine then no longer helps against them.
107269.m: Resistant bacteria can no longer be fought with the antibiotic.

107270.q: What does the cap of a common morel look like?
a: Like a honeycomb with lots of pits
Smooth and red with white spots
107270.e: The cap of the common morel is covered with ridges and deep pits. It looks like a honeycomb or a sponge.
107270.m: The common morel has a honeycomb-like cap.

107271.q: In which season does the common morel grow?
107271.e: Morels usually appear between March and May. This makes them some of the first edible mushrooms of the year.

107272.q: Why must you not eat common morels raw?
a: They are too sour when raw
They are rock hard when raw
107272.e: Raw morels contain substances that can cause poisoning. Only thorough cooking makes them safe to eat.
107272.m: Morels must always be cooked thoroughly.

107273.q: Which poisonous mushroom can be confused with the common morel?
107273.e: The false morel also grows in spring. But its cap is folded like a brain rather than like a honeycomb, and it is poisonous.
107273.m: The poisonous false morel looks like the morel.

107274.q: What does the inside of a common morel look like when you cut it lengthways?
107274.e: The cap and stalk of the common morel together form a single hollow space. This helps to tell it apart from lookalikes.
107274.m: A common morel is hollow inside.

107275.q: How does the common morel reproduce?
107275.e: Like all fungi, the morel forms tiny spores. In the morel they form in small sacs, which is why it belongs to the sac fungi.

107276.q: Why are dried morels in the shops particularly expensive?
a: They are rare and hard to find
They grow only every ten years
107276.e: Morels grow only for a short time in spring and are well camouflaged. They are also very hard to cultivate, which keeps the price high.
107276.m: Morels are rare and therefore expensive.

107277.q: Under which tree are morels often found in Switzerland?
107277.e: Morels like to grow in floodplain forests, at the edges of woods and under ash trees. They also often appear where fires have been.
107277.m: Morels are often found under ash trees.

107278.e: Truffles form their lumpy fruiting bodies in the soil. That is why you cannot see them from outside.

107279.q: Which animals are mostly used to search for truffles today?
107279.e: Trained truffle dogs can smell the ripe truffles in the soil. In the past, pigs were also used, but they like to eat the truffles themselves.
107279.m: Today truffles are mostly searched for with dogs.

107280.q: How do truffles spread their spores even though they grow underground?
a: Their smell attracts animals that eat them
The wind blows them out of the ground
They burst and fling the spores up high
Earthworms carry them into the trees
107280.e: Ripe truffles give off a strong smell. Animals such as wild boar dig them up, eat them and pass the spores out somewhere else.
107280.m: The smell of truffles attracts animals that spread their spores.

107281.q: Which truffle from Piedmont is considered the most expensive in the world?
107281.e: The white truffle from the area around Alba can hardly be cultivated and is almost only gathered in the wild. Several thousand francs are often paid for one kilogram.
107281.m: The white Alba truffle is the most expensive truffle.

107282.q: Which country does the well-known black Périgord truffle come from?
107282.e: The Périgord truffle is named after a region in south-western France. It is harvested in winter.
107282.m: The Périgord truffle comes from France.

107283.q: Which kind of truffle is most common in Switzerland?
107283.e: In Switzerland, it is mainly the Burgundy truffle that grows, for example in the Jura and on the Swiss Plateau. It is harvested in autumn.
107283.m: The most common truffle in Switzerland is the Burgundy truffle.

107284.q: With the roots of which trees do truffles often form a partnership?
107284.e: Truffles form a mycorrhiza with broadleaved trees such as oaks, beeches and hazel bushes. Without these trees they cannot grow.
107284.m: Truffles live in partnership with oaks and hazel bushes.

107285.q: What is a planting of trees called, on whose roots truffles are meant to grow?
107285.e: Young trees whose roots have been inoculated with truffle fungus are planted. It often takes many years until the first harvest.
107285.m: Truffles can be grown in orchards with inoculated trees.

107286.q: Why do you cut off the stalk before making a spore print?
a: So that the cap lies flat on the paper
So that the mushroom grows faster
Because the stalk eats the spores
107286.e: Without the stalk, you can lay the cap with its underside straight on the paper. The spores then fall a short distance and form a sharp pattern.
107286.m: For a spore print, you remove the stalk.

107287.q: What is a spore print used for when identifying mushrooms?
a: It shows the colour of the spore powder
It measures the weight of the mushroom
It shows the age of the mushroom
107287.e: The colour of the spore powder is an important feature. It often helps to tell similar-looking mushrooms apart.
107287.m: The spore print shows the spore colour of the mushroom.

107288.q: Why do you cover the mushroom cap with a glass or bowl when making a spore print?
a: So that no draught blows the spores away
So that the spores stay warm
So that the mushroom does not glow
107288.e: The spores are very light. Even a slight draught would smudge the fine pattern.
107288.m: When making a spore print, a cover protects against draughts.

107289.q: Why is paper that is half white and half black often used for a spore print?
a: Both light and dark spores can then be seen well
So that the paper does not get wet
So that the mushroom dries faster
Because spores only fall onto black
107289.e: White spore powder is hard to see on white paper. It becomes visible on the dark part, while dark powder shows up on the light part.
107289.m: On two-coloured paper you can see both light and dark spores.

107290.q: What colour is the spore powder of the death cap?
107290.e: The poisonous death cap leaves a white spore print. Button mushrooms, with which it is confused, do not have white spore powder.
107290.m: The death cap has white spore powder.

107291.q: What can you use to make a finished spore print last?
107291.e: The spore powder only lies loosely on the paper. A fine mist of hairspray or fixative spray sticks it down.
107291.m: You can fix a spore print with hairspray.

107292.q: What does the pattern of a successful spore print from a gilled mushroom show?
a: Lines radiating out like the gills
107292.e: The spores fall down exactly between the gills. That is why a pattern radiating outwards forms on the paper.
107292.m: A spore print traces the gills as a radiating pattern.

107293.q: About how long must a mushroom cap lie on the paper before a spore print becomes visible?
107293.e: The mushroom drops its spores little by little. It is usually left for a few hours or overnight.
107293.m: A spore print takes a few hours.

107294.q: Does cooking make the poison of the death cap harmless?
a: No, it stays deadly even when cooked
Yes, after five minutes of cooking
Yes, if you dry the mushroom
107294.e: The poison amanitin is not destroyed by boiling, frying or drying. Even a single mushroom can be deadly.
107294.m: The poison of the death cap stays dangerous even when cooked.

107295.q: How can you recognise the poisonous fly agaric?
a: By its red cap with white flakes
By its brown cap with tubes
By its all-white cap with no spots
107295.e: The fly agaric has a bright red cap with white flakes. It contains poisons that affect the nervous system.
107295.m: The fly agaric has a red cap with white flakes.

107296.q: What are health problems called that come from actually edible mushrooms that were spoilt or stored wrongly?
107296.e: Edible mushrooms also spoil quickly because they contain a lot of protein and water. Old mushrooms or those stored for a long time in plastic can cause stomach and bowel problems.
107296.m: Spoilt edible mushrooms can cause false mushroom poisoning.

107297.q: When should you get medical help if you suspect mushroom poisoning?
a: Only if you have a fever
Only if several people fall ill
107297.e: With some poisonous mushrooms, symptoms appear late, when organs are already damaged. The earlier treatment starts, the better the chances.
107297.m: If you suspect mushroom poisoning, get help at once.

107298.q: What do official mushroom inspectors do?
a: They check gathered mushrooms to see if they are edible
They plant mushrooms in the forest
They sell mushrooms at the market
They count the trees in the forest
107298.e: In many municipalities you can have gathered mushrooms checked for free. The experts sort out the poisonous ones.
107298.m: The mushroom inspection checks whether gathered mushrooms are edible.

107299.q: Is the old rule true that a silver spoon turns black with poisonous mushrooms?
a: No, that is a dangerous myth
107299.e: No household test can reliably detect poisonous mushrooms. The death cap, for example, does not discolour silver.
107299.m: Only careful identification protects against poisonous mushrooms, not a silver spoon.

107300.q: Why are some cases of mushroom poisoning particularly treacherous?
a: The symptoms appear only after days
107300.e: With some poisonous mushrooms, such as the fool's webcap, the symptoms appear only after several days. By then organs such as the kidneys are often already damaged.
107300.m: Some mushroom poisons only take effect after days.

107301.q: How are most wild mushrooms eaten so that they are easy to digest?
107301.e: Many edible mushrooms are hard to digest or even slightly poisonous when raw. Cooking them well makes them safe to eat.
107301.m: Wild mushrooms are eaten well cooked.

107302.q: Which poisonous mushroom can be confused with the chanterelle?
107302.e: The orange jack-o'-lantern mushroom grows in clusters on wood and has real, thin gills. It causes violent vomiting and diarrhoea.
107302.m: The poisonous jack-o'-lantern mushroom looks like the chanterelle.

107303.q: What is a mushroom closed season?
a: A time when picking mushrooms is forbidden
The time when mushrooms grow fastest
The rest period after a mushroom meal
The time when mushrooms are cooked
107303.e: During a closed season, no mushrooms may be picked. In many places, this applies on certain days of the month.
107303.m: During the mushroom closed season, picking mushrooms is forbidden.

107304.q: Who sets the rules for picking mushrooms in Switzerland, for example closed days and maximum amounts?
107304.e: Mushroom picking is regulated by the cantons. That is why closed days and permitted amounts differ from canton to canton.
107304.m: In Switzerland, the rules for picking mushrooms are a matter for the cantons.

107305.q: Why are mushrooms in nature reserves often completely protected from picking?
a: Plants, fungi and animals are specially protected there
The mushrooms there are too small
The mushrooms there belong to the forester
107305.e: In protected areas, nature is meant to stay as undisturbed as possible. That is why picking is often forbidden there.
107305.m: Picking mushrooms is often forbidden in nature reserves.

107306.q: Where is picking mushrooms completely forbidden in Switzerland?
107306.e: In the Swiss National Park in the Engadine, you may not take away any plants or mushrooms. Nature is meant to develop undisturbed there.
107306.m: Picking mushrooms is forbidden in the Swiss National Park.

107307.q: What did a long-term study by the WSL research institute show about picking mushrooms?
a: Trampling does more harm than picking
Picking makes the mycelium die at once
Mushrooms only grow if you pick them
Mushrooms only grow when there is snow
107307.e: In mushroom reserves in the canton of Fribourg, such as La Chanéaz, observations were made for about 30 years. Picking did not reduce the number of fruiting bodies, but heavy trampling of the forest floor did, even if only for a while.
107307.m: When picking mushrooms, trampling the ground does more harm than picking.

107308.q: Why are there closed days and limits on amounts for picking mushrooms?
a: To protect the mushrooms and the forest floor
Because mushrooms become poisonous at night
107308.e: Protective rules are meant to reduce the pressure from picking. That way mushrooms can spread their spores, and the forest floor and animals are spared.
107308.m: Closed days protect the mushrooms and the forest.

107309.q: What should you do with small, young and old mushrooms when picking?
107309.e: Very young mushrooms are hard to identify, and old ones are often spoilt. If left standing, they can spread spores.
107309.m: Leave young and old mushrooms standing.

107310.q: What is the right way to behave towards poisonous mushrooms in the forest?
107310.e: Poisonous mushrooms are also important for the forest, for example as partners of trees and as food for animals. Anyone who stamps on them harms nature.
107310.m: Leave poisonous mushrooms standing in the forest.

107311.q: With which food can you generously cut away a small mouldy spot?
107311.e: Hard cheese is so firm that the fungal network can hardly spread. You cut the spot away with a margin of about one centimetre; soft or runny foods, on the other hand, are thrown away.
107311.m: You may only cut mould away from firm foods such as hard cheese.

107312.q: How are truffles mostly used in cooking?
107312.e: Truffles have a very strong aroma that is lost with long cooking. That is why they are usually shaved finely over a finished dish such as pasta or risotto.
107312.m: Truffles are usually shaved raw over the finished dish.

107409.q: Roughly what share of the total blood volume is blood plasma?
107409.e: Blood is around 55 per cent liquid plasma. The rest is made up of blood cells.
107409.m: A little more than half of the blood is liquid plasma.

107410.q: What is the liquid, yellowish part of the blood without the blood cells called?
107410.e: If blood is left to stand or is spun in a centrifuge, the cells settle at the bottom. The yellowish blood plasma stays on top.
107410.m: Blood plasma is the liquid part of the blood.

107411.q: What is blood plasma mostly made of?
107411.e: Blood plasma is about nine tenths water. Proteins, salts, nutrients and hormones are dissolved in it.

107412.q: Which device is used in the laboratory to separate plasma from blood cells?
107412.e: The centrifuge spins the tube very fast. The heavy cells sink to the bottom, and the lighter plasma stays on top.
107412.m: A centrifuge separates blood cells and plasma by spinning fast.

107413.q: Which substances, among others, are carried dissolved in blood plasma?
107413.e: Dissolved substances such as sugar, fats, salts and hormones float in the plasma. In this way they reach all the cells.
107413.m: Blood plasma carries dissolved nutrients and hormones all over the body.

107414.q: What, among other things, is donated blood plasma used for?
107414.e: Donated plasma is used to obtain albumin, antibodies and clotting factors, for example. These medicines help many sick people.
107414.m: Important medicines are made from donated plasma.

107415.q: What happens to the blood cells when you donate plasma?
a: They flow back into the body
107415.e: A machine separates the plasma and gives the blood cells back to the donor. That is why you can donate plasma more often than whole blood.
107415.m: When you donate plasma, you get the blood cells back.

107416.q: What are the defence substances in blood plasma that recognise germs called?
107416.e: Antibodies are proteins dissolved in the plasma. They recognise germs and mark them for the defence cells.
107416.m: Antibodies in the blood recognise germs.

107417.q: Which animal is the Rhesus factor named after?
107417.e: The feature was discovered in experiments with blood from rhesus monkeys. That is where the name comes from.
107417.m: The Rhesus factor is named after the rhesus monkey.

107418.q: What does “Rhesus positive” mean in a person?
a: A certain feature sits on the red blood cells
The blood contains no white blood cells
The blood contains especially a lot of iron
107418.e: Rhesus positive means that the red blood cells carry the Rhesus feature. If it is missing, you are Rhesus negative.
107418.m: Rhesus-positive people have the Rhesus feature on their red blood cells.

107419.q: Roughly how many people in Europe are Rhesus positive?
107419.e: Around 85 out of 100 people in Europe are Rhesus positive. Only about 15 per cent are Rhesus negative.
107419.m: Most people in Europe are Rhesus positive.

107420.q: Does a Rhesus-negative person have antibodies against feature D from birth?
a: No, only after contact with Rhesus-positive blood
Only if they have blood group A
107420.e: Anti-D antibodies only form when the immune system meets Rhesus-positive blood. This process is called sensitisation.
107420.m: The body only makes antibodies against the Rhesus feature after contact.

107421.q: Why should a Rhesus-negative person not be given Rhesus-positive blood?
a: They can form antibodies that destroy the foreign blood cells
It gives them a fever straight away
Their heart then beats too slowly
107421.e: The immune system recognises the foreign feature D and forms antibodies. In a later transfusion, the donor cells are then attacked.
107421.m: Rhesus-negative people should only be given Rhesus-negative blood.

107422.q: How do you write blood group A with a positive Rhesus factor in short?
107422.e: The plus sign after the blood group stands for Rhesus positive. A minus sign means Rhesus negative.
107422.m: The plus sign with the blood group means Rhesus positive.

a: Yes, it is inherited from the parents
No, it depends on where you live
107423.e: The Rhesus factor is fixed by the genes and is passed on from parents to children. It stays the same for life.
107423.m: The Rhesus factor is inborn and stays the same for life.

107424.q: Which blood group counts as the universal recipient for red blood cells?
107424.e: People with AB positive have no antibodies against A, B or D. That is why they can be given red blood cells of all groups.
107424.m: People with AB positive can be given red blood cells of all groups.

107425.q: Why can red blood cells of group O be given to many people?
a: They carry no A and no B features
107425.e: The recipient’s antibodies are directed against the features A and B. If these are missing from the cells, there is no clumping.
107425.m: Red blood cells of group O have no A and B features.

107426.q: Which antibodies does a person with blood group O have in their plasma?
107426.e: With blood group O, the features A and B are missing from the cells. That is why the body makes antibodies against both.
107426.m: People with blood group O have antibodies against A and against B.

107427.q: Which antibodies does a person with blood group A have in their plasma?
107427.e: The body does not make antibodies against its own feature A. But it does have antibodies against the foreign feature B.
107427.m: People with blood group A have antibodies against B.

107428.q: Plasma from which blood group is suitable for all recipients?
107428.e: Plasma from group AB contains neither anti-A nor anti-B. That is why it does not attack the cells of any recipient.
107428.m: For plasma, blood group AB is the universal donor.

107429.q: From which blood groups can a person with blood group B be given red blood cells?
107429.e: A person with group B has anti-A in their plasma. So they can only take cells without feature A, which means from B and O.
107429.m: People with blood group B can take red blood cells from B and O.

107430.q: Which blood group is the rarest in Switzerland?
107430.e: Only around one per cent of the population has AB negative. The groups A positive and O positive are the most common.
107430.m: AB negative is the rarest blood group in Switzerland.

107431.q: Why is group O negative blood especially in demand at blood donation services?
a: It is given in emergencies before the blood group is known
107431.e: After serious accidents, there is often no time to find out the blood group. Then injured people are given group O negative blood first.
107431.m: In emergencies, group O negative blood is often used first.

107432.q: From which blood group can a person with O negative be given red blood cells?
a: From O positive and O negative
From A negative and O negative
107432.e: People with O negative have antibodies against A and B and can form antibodies against D. That is why they can only take cells without A, B and D.
107432.m: People with O negative can only take red blood cells from O negative.

107433.q: What happens if someone is given red blood cells of an unsuitable blood group?
a: The blood cells clump together and are destroyed
The blood turns green straight away
The body makes new bones straight away
107433.e: The recipient’s antibodies attach to the foreign cells. These clump together and break apart, which can be life-threatening.
107433.m: With the wrong blood group, the blood cells clump together dangerously.

107434.q: What must match before a blood transfusion?
a: The blood groups of donor and recipient
107434.e: If the blood group does not match, the blood can clump together. That is why it is checked again right beside the patient before every transfusion.
107434.m: In a transfusion, the blood group must match.

107435.q: Why is a little donor blood mixed with the recipient’s blood in the laboratory before a transfusion?
107435.e: If the mixture does not clump, the two blood samples are compatible. This laboratory test is called cross-matching.
107435.m: Before a transfusion, a test checks whether the blood is compatible.

107436.q: Which organisation collects blood donations in Switzerland?
107436.e: The Blood Transfusion Service SRC Switzerland is part of the Swiss Red Cross. Together with regional services, it organises blood donations.
107436.m: In Switzerland, the Blood Transfusion Service of the Swiss Red Cross organises blood donation.

107437.q: What is it called when a person has their own blood taken before a planned operation?
107437.e: In autologous blood donation, your own blood is stored and given back if needed. This avoids any problems with other people’s blood groups.
107437.m: In autologous blood donation, you later get your own blood back.

107438.q: Why is donated blood usually split into its parts?
a: Each patient only gets the part they need
107438.e: Red blood cells, plasma and sometimes platelets are obtained from one donation. In this way one donation often helps several people.
107438.m: A blood donation is split up and can therefore help several people.

107439.q: What is a red cell concentrate?
a: A bag of stored red blood cells
A device for measuring the pulse
107439.e: For a red cell concentrate, the red blood cells are separated from a donation. It is the blood product that is transfused most often.
107439.m: A red cell concentrate mainly contains red blood cells.

107440.q: What is every blood donation tested for in the laboratory before it is used?
a: Germs such as HIV and hepatitis
107440.e: Every donation is tested for blood group and for diseases that can be passed on. This prevents germs being passed to recipients.
107440.m: Every blood donation is checked for germs before it is used.

107442.q: Roughly how many red blood cells does one microlitre of blood contain in adults?
107442.e: A tiny droplet of one microlitre contains around 4 to 6 million red blood cells. They are the most common blood cells.
107442.m: Red blood cells are the most common cells in the blood.

107443.q: What is examined in a blood count?
107443.e: In a blood count, the laboratory counts red and white blood cells and platelets. This can show anaemia or infections, for example.
107443.m: A blood count shows which cells are in the blood.

107444.q: What does the abbreviation “Hb” stand for in a blood count?
107444.e: Hb stands for haemoglobin, the red pigment in blood. A low Hb level can point to anaemia.
107444.m: In a blood count, Hb stands for the red pigment haemoglobin.

107445.q: Are there more red or more white blood cells in the blood?
107445.e: In a tiny drop of blood there are around a thousand times more red than white blood cells. The white ones are still important for the body’s defences.
107445.m: There are far more red than white blood cells in the blood.

107446.q: Why does the doctor sometimes do a blood count when you have an infection?
a: She can see whether there are more white blood cells
She wants to find out the hair colour
She uses it to measure body weight
She uses it to test hearing
107446.e: During an infection, the body makes more white blood cells for defence. The blood count shows this change.
107446.m: With infections, the number of white blood cells often rises.

107447.q: What do scavenger cells in the blood do?
a: They eat bacteria and foreign bodies
107447.e: Scavenger cells are a kind of white blood cell. They take up bacteria and destroy them.

107448.q: Which blood cells protect the body from germs?
107448.e: White blood cells are the body’s defence cells. Some eat germs, others make antibodies.
107448.m: White blood cells are the police in the blood.

107449.q: Which blood cells are called erythrocytes in a blood count?
107449.e: The name comes from the Greek “erythros”, meaning red. In a blood count they are counted and their size is measured.
107449.m: Erythrocytes are the red blood cells.

107450.q: Where are new red blood cells made?
107450.e: Billions of new red blood cells are made in the bone marrow every day. They replace the old ones, which are broken down after about 120 days.
107450.m: Red blood cells are made in the bone marrow.

107451.e: Platelets are pieces pinched off from larger cells. That is why they have no nucleus of their own.

107452.q: Where in the body are platelets made?
107452.e: In the bone marrow, many small platelets are pinched off from large cells. The other blood cells are made there too.
107452.m: Platelets are made in the bone marrow.

107454.q: What happens if someone has too few platelets?
a: They bruise and bleed more easily
They get a fever straight away
They see less well at night
107454.e: Without enough platelets, the blood clots less well. Even small knocks then cause bruises, and wounds bleed for longer.
107454.m: Too few platelets lead to more bleeding.

107455.q: Roughly how long does a platelet live?
a: About a week to ten days
107455.e: Platelets have a short life of around a week. That is why the bone marrow constantly has to make new ones.
107455.m: Platelets only live for about a week.

107456.q: Which well-known medicine stops platelets working and is therefore used to help prevent heart attacks?
107456.e: Acetylsalicylic acid, known as aspirin, stops platelets from sticking together. In a small dose it can prevent blood clots in the vessels.
107456.m: Aspirin stops platelets from sticking together.

107457.q: In which organ are old platelets mainly broken down?
107457.e: The spleen filters aged blood cells out of the blood. Most old platelets are broken down there too.
107457.m: Old platelets are mainly broken down in the spleen.

a: A blood product made from donated platelets
A device for measuring blood pressure
A test to find out the blood group
107458.e: Platelet concentrates are given, for example, to people after chemotherapy who have too few platelets of their own. They help to prevent bleeding.
107458.m: A platelet concentrate contains donated platelets.

107459.q: What forms in a wound so that it stops bleeding?
107459.e: When you are injured, the blood clots. Fine threads of fibrin form a net, and a plug forms that closes the wound.

107460.q: Which small parts of the blood help fibrin to close a wound?
107460.e: Platelets gather at the wound and stick together. Together with the fibrin net, they form a firm plug.

107461.q: What shape does fibrin form in a wound?
107461.e: Fibrin threads join up into a dense net. Blood cells get caught in it, and a firm plug forms.
107461.m: Fibrin forms a net in which blood cells get caught.

107462.q: In which organ is fibrinogen made?
107462.e: The liver makes many plasma proteins, including fibrinogen and other clotting factors. That is why clotting can be disturbed in liver diseases.
107462.m: The liver makes many substances for blood clotting.

107463.q: What happens to the blood clot once the wound has healed?
107463.e: After healing, the body breaks down the fibrin net again. This process is called fibrinolysis.
107463.m: The body dissolves blood clots again after healing.

107465.q: What do surgeons use fibrin glue for?
a: To seal wounds and stop bleeding
107465.e: Fibrin glue copies the last step of blood clotting. It makes a firm clot form on the wound and sticks tissue together.
107465.m: Fibrin glue closes wounds like naturally clotted blood.

107466.q: Why can a small cut stop bleeding after a few minutes?
a: The blood clots and seals it
The heart stops beating for a moment
107466.e: When you are injured, the blood clots. Threads of fibrin form a net and seal the wound.

107467.q: What is the medical term for the bleeding disorder in which blood clots too slowly?
107467.e: In haemophilia, the blood clots too slowly. Even small injuries can therefore bleed for a long time.
107467.m: The medical name for this bleeding disorder is haemophilia.

107468.q: What does not work properly in haemophilia?
107468.e: In haemophilia, the blood clots too slowly. A wound therefore closes only poorly.
107468.m: In haemophilia, the blood clots poorly.

107469.q: What is missing in the blood of people with haemophilia?
107469.e: In haemophilia, a particular protein needed for blood clotting is missing. That is why bleeding is slow to stop.
107469.m: In haemophilia, a clotting substance is missing from the blood.

107470.q: Why do many more boys and men have haemophilia?
a: The gene is on the X chromosome
107470.e: Men have only one X chromosome. If the gene on it is changed, there is no second X to make up for the fault.
107470.m: Haemophilia is inherited via the X chromosome and mainly affects men.

107471.q: Why was haemophilia once called a disease of royal families?
a: It appeared in several European royal families
Only kings were allowed to treat it
You got it from wearing a crown
Only rich people could get it
107471.e: Britain's Queen Victoria carried the gene. Through her descendants, the disease reached the royal families of Spain, Russia and Prussia.
107471.m: Haemophilia spread through European royal families.

107472.q: Can you catch haemophilia from someone?
a: No, people are born with it
107472.e: Haemophilia is passed on through the genes. People have it from birth and cannot infect anyone.
107472.m: Haemophilia is present from birth and is not contagious.

107473.q: How is haemophilia mostly treated today?
a: With injections of the missing clotting factor
With lots of exercise in the sun
With a brace on the teeth
107473.e: People with haemophilia inject the missing factor into a vein regularly or when needed. This lets many of them lead an almost normal life.
107473.m: In haemophilia, the missing clotting factor is injected.

107474.q: Why must people with haemophilia be careful in sports with lots of falls?
a: Even small injuries can bleed for a long time
107474.e: Because the blood clots poorly, bruises can lead to heavy internal bleeding. Swimming or cycling with protection are often good choices.
107474.m: With haemophilia, even small injuries can bleed for a long time.

107475.q: Where does internal bleeding happen especially often in severe haemophilia?
107475.e: Bleeding into the knee, elbow and ankle joints is typical. Without treatment, the joints can be permanently damaged.
107475.m: In haemophilia, the joints often bleed.

107476.q: What does the word “leukaemia” literally mean?
107476.e: The word comes from Greek: “leukos” means white and “haima” means blood. In severe illness the blood can look paler.

107477.q: Which cells multiply out of control in leukaemia?
107477.e: In leukaemia, huge numbers of immature white blood cells are made. They cannot do their jobs and crowd out healthy blood cells.
107477.m: In leukaemia, immature white blood cells multiply out of control.

107478.q: Which type of cancer is most common in children?
107478.e: About a third of all cancers in children are leukaemias. Today most children can be cured.
107478.m: Leukaemia is the most common cancer in children.

107479.q: Why do people donate stem cells for leukaemia patients?
a: So the patients can make healthy blood again
107479.e: In some leukaemias, the diseased bone marrow is replaced. Healthy stem cells from a donor then make healthy blood cells again.
107479.m: Donated stem cells can help leukaemia patients.

107480.q: Which treatment do people with leukaemia receive most often?
107480.e: In chemotherapy, medicines destroy the cancer cells. Depending on the type, other treatments are added.
107480.m: Leukaemia is mostly treated with chemotherapy.

107481.q: Where in the body are the blood cells made that are diseased in leukaemia?
107481.e: Blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft inside of the bones. In leukaemia, too many immature white blood cells are made there.
107481.m: Leukaemia starts in the bone marrow.

107482.q: Why are people with leukaemia often pale and tired?
a: Because too few red blood cells are made
Because they get too much sun
Because their heart is too big
107482.e: The cancer cells crowd out the making of healthy blood cells. With too few red blood cells, less oxygen reaches the body.
107482.m: Leukaemia crowds out healthy blood cells and therefore makes people tired.

107483.q: Which leukaemia is most common in older adults in Europe?
107483.e: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, CLL for short, often develops slowly over years. It mainly occurs in people over 60.
107483.m: In older people, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is the most common.

107484.q: Which condition can a severe lack of iron cause?
107484.e: Without enough iron, the body cannot make enough haemoglobin. This leads to iron deficiency anaemia.
107484.m: A lack of iron can lead to anaemia.

107485.q: Which vitamin improves the absorption of iron from plant foods?
107485.e: Vitamin C helps the gut absorb iron from plants better. A glass of orange juice with lentils is therefore a good idea.
107485.m: Vitamin C helps the body absorb iron.

107486.q: Roughly how much iron does an adult's body contain?
107486.e: An adult has only around 3 to 5 grams of iron, about as much as in a small nail. Most of it is in haemoglobin.
107486.m: The body contains only a few grams of iron.

107487.q: Why do you often feel tired when you lack iron?
107487.e: Iron is part of the red blood pigment that carries oxygen. Without enough iron, muscles and brain get less oxygen.
107487.m: A lack of iron makes you tired because less oxygen is carried.

107488.q: Which of these plant foods contains a lot of iron?
107488.e: Pulses such as lentils are good plant sources of iron. Cucumbers and apples, on the other hand, contain little iron.
107488.m: Lentils are a good plant source of iron.

107489.q: Which animal food contains a lot of iron?
107489.e: Red meat such as beef contains a lot of iron that the body can absorb well. Butter, cream and honey contain hardly any iron.
107489.m: Red meat is a good source of iron.

107490.q: Which drink with a meal can reduce the absorption of iron?
107490.e: Tannins in black tea bind iron in the gut. So it is better not to drink it right with iron-rich meals.
107490.m: Black tea with a meal reduces iron absorption.

107491.q: What does the hormone insulin do in the blood?
107491.e: Insulin makes sure that sugar moves from the blood into the cells. This lowers the blood sugar level.

107493.q: Where does the blood get sugar from when you have not eaten for a long time?
107493.e: The liver stores sugar as a reserve. When you do not eat for a long time, it releases some into the blood so that blood sugar does not drop too low.
107493.m: The liver is the body's sugar store.

107494.q: What is the illness called in which blood sugar is permanently too high?
107494.e: In diabetes, insulin is missing or does not work well enough. So too much sugar stays in the blood.
107494.m: In diabetes mellitus, blood sugar is permanently too high.

107495.q: What helps quickly when blood sugar is too low?
a: Glucose tablets or a sugary drink
107495.e: When blood sugar is too low, the brain needs energy fast. Glucose or sugary drinks get into the blood quickly.
107495.m: Glucose helps quickly when blood sugar is too low.

107496.q: Why was the discovery of insulin in 1921 so important?
a: Since then diabetes can be treated
Since then broken bones can be healed
Since then there have been vaccines
Since then people can donate blood
107496.e: Before that, people with type 1 diabetes often died young. With insulin they can live well today.
107496.m: Thanks to insulin, diabetes can be treated.

107497.q: Where in the body is the pancreas, which makes insulin?
a: In the belly behind the stomach
In the head behind the eyes
In the neck next to the larynx
In the leg next to the knee
107497.e: The pancreas lies across the upper belly behind the stomach. It makes insulin and digestive juices.
107497.m: The pancreas lies behind the stomach.

107498.q: Which type of diabetes usually starts in childhood or the teenage years?
107498.e: In type 1 diabetes, the body's own immune system destroys the cells that make insulin. People with it need insulin for the rest of their lives.
107498.m: Type 1 diabetes often starts in children and teenagers.

107499.q: What do many people with diabetes use to check their own blood sugar?
a: A blood glucose meter or sensor
107499.e: A blood glucose meter measures the sugar in a drop of blood from the fingertip. Modern sensors on the skin measure all the time.
107499.m: People with diabetes often measure their blood sugar themselves.

107500.q: What did Karl Landsteiner observe when he mixed blood from different people?
107500.e: Landsteiner saw that some blood samples mix well and others clump together. This is how he discovered the blood groups.
107500.m: Blood that does not match clumps together.

107501.q: Which prize did Karl Landsteiner receive in 1930?
107501.e: For discovering the human blood groups, Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1930.
107501.m: Karl Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1930.

107502.q: Which international day takes place on Karl Landsteiner's birthday, 14 June?
107502.e: World Blood Donor Day honours Landsteiner, who was born on 14 June 1868. On this day, blood donors are thanked.
107502.m: World Blood Donor Day is on 14 June.

107503.q: What did Karl Landsteiner discover around the year 1900?
107503.e: Karl Landsteiner found out that people have different blood groups. He later received the Nobel Prize for this.
107503.m: Karl Landsteiner discovered the blood groups.

107504.q: Why is Landsteiner's discovery so important for blood transfusions?
a: Not all blood suits every person
107504.e: If someone receives blood of an unsuitable blood group, it can be life-threatening. Since Landsteiner, the blood group is checked before every transfusion.
107504.m: Before a blood transfusion, the blood group must match.

107505.q: Which further blood group feature did Landsteiner describe in 1940 together with Alexander Wiener?
107505.e: Together with Wiener, Landsteiner found an additional feature of red blood cells in 1940. This made transfusions even safer.
107505.m: Landsteiner also helped discover the rhesus factor.

107506.q: Which blood group exists besides A, B and AB?
107506.e: In Karl Landsteiner's system there are the blood groups A, B, AB and O. He first called group O “C”.
107506.m: The blood groups are A, B, AB and O.

107507.e: Landsteiner studied medicine in Vienna and worked as a doctor and researcher in pathology. He made his discoveries in the laboratory.
107507.m: Karl Landsteiner was a doctor and researcher.

107607.q: What do spore plants such as ferns and mosses never form?
107607.e: Spore plants reproduce with spores instead of seeds. They do not form flowers. They are also called cryptogams.
107607.m: Spore plants have no flowers and no seeds.

107608.q: What is the basic difference between a spore and a seed?
a: It usually consists of only one cell
It always has a hard fruit case
It forms only in a flower
107608.e: A seed contains a small embryo and food tissue. A spore is usually just a single cell with a protective wall.
107608.m: A spore is built much more simply than a seed.

107609.q: Which of these plant groups does NOT belong to the spore plants?
107609.e: Conifers form seeds in cones and belong to the seed plants. Clubmosses, horsetails and mosses reproduce with spores.
107609.m: Conifers are seed plants, not spore plants.

107610.q: What are ferns, horsetails and clubmosses called together?
107610.e: Ferns, horsetails and clubmosses together form the pteridophytes. Unlike mosses, they have vascular bundles, but they have no seeds.
107610.m: Ferns, horsetails and clubmosses belong to the pteridophytes.

107611.q: How long ago did the first plants begin to colonise dry land?
107611.e: The first land plants were moss-like spore plants and appeared in the Palaeozoic era over 400 million years ago. Flowering plants came much later.
107611.m: The first land plants were spore plants.

107612.q: Why are spores still found in rocks after millions of years?
a: They keep growing in the rock
They are formed anew every year
107612.e: The outer wall of spores is made of sporopollenin, one of the most durable natural substances of all. That is why spores last a very long time.
107612.m: Spores are protected by a very stable wall.

107613.q: Why are fungi no longer counted as plants today, even though they form spores?
a: They form a kingdom of their own
107613.e: Fungi have no chlorophyll and feed on other substances. That is why they form a kingdom of their own alongside plants and animals.
107613.m: Fungi are neither plants nor animals.

107614.q: Which spore plant often grows across the forest floor with long, creeping shoots?
107614.e: The stag's-horn clubmoss forms creeping shoots metres long with small leaves on the ground. Clubmosses are protected in many areas.
107614.m: Clubmosses creep across the forest floor with long shoots.

107615.q: What is meant by alternation of generations in mosses and ferns?
a: A spore-forming and a sex-cell-forming generation take turns
Old plants die off completely every winter
Young plants always grow in the shade of the old ones
The plants change where they grow every year
107615.e: From a spore grows a generation that forms sex cells. From the fertilised egg cell grows a generation that forms spores again.
107615.m: In alternation of generations, two different generations follow one another.

107616.q: Where does a fern form its spores?
a: In brown clusters on the underside of the fronds
107616.e: Small brown clusters sit on the underside of fern fronds. The spores form inside them and are spread by the wind.
107616.m: Ferns form their spores on the underside of the fronds.

107617.q: What grows from a spore in a fern?
a: Straight away a large fern with fronds
107617.e: From the spore, a tiny, usually heart-shaped prothallus grows first. The sex cells form on it, and from them a new fern later grows.
107617.m: From a fern spore, a prothallus grows first.

107618.q: Which generation is the green moss plant you see in the forest?
107618.e: In mosses, the green plant is the generation with the sex cells. The spore capsule on its stalk is the other generation.
107618.m: In mosses, the green plant is the generation with the sex cells.

107619.q: Which generation is the large plant with fronds in ferns?
107619.e: In ferns it is the other way round from mosses. The eye-catching plant with fronds forms spores, while the generation with the sex cells is only tiny.
107619.m: In ferns, the large plant is the spore-forming generation.

107620.q: In true mosses, what does the stalk with the spore capsule feed on?
a: The green moss plant it sits on
107620.e: The spore capsule with its stalk grows on the moss plant and is supplied with nutrients by it. So it is not independent.
107620.m: The spore capsule of mosses lives on the green moss plant.

107621.q: How do mosses and ferns reproduce, since they have no flowers?
107621.e: Mosses and ferns form no flowers and no seeds. They spread with tiny spores that the wind carries away.
107621.m: Mosses and ferns reproduce with spores.

107622.q: In ferns, what grows from the fertilised egg cell?
a: A young fern plant with fronds
A spore capsule on a stalk
A small bulb in the ground
107622.e: The fertilised egg cell first develops on the prothallus. From it grows a young fern plant, which later forms spores itself.
107622.m: In ferns, a new fern plant grows from the fertilised egg cell.

107623.q: What do mosses and ferns need for fertilisation to work?
a: Water, for example rain or dew
Lots of sun and dry weather
107623.e: The male sex cells of mosses and ferns swim to the egg cell. For this they need a film of water, which is why these plants often grow in damp places.
107623.m: Mosses and ferns need water for fertilisation.

107624.q: What grows first out of a fern spore?
a: Straight away a large fern frond
107624.e: From the spore, a tiny green plate grows first, the prothallus. Only later does the young fern plant with fronds grow from it.
107624.m: From a fern spore, a prothallus grows first.

107625.q: In mosses, what grows first from a spore?
a: A fine green network of threads
107625.e: From the moss spore, a branched green network of threads grows first. Only from this do the small moss plants grow.
107625.m: In mosses, a green network of threads grows first from the spore.

107626.q: What shape is the prothallus of many ferns?
107626.e: The prothallus of many ferns is a flat, green, heart-shaped plate. It lies close to the damp ground.
107626.m: The fern prothallus is often a small, heart-shaped plate.

107627.q: How big is the prothallus of a fern usually?
a: As big as the palm of a hand
107627.e: The prothallus is usually only a few millimetres to about one centimetre across. That is why it is easily overlooked in nature.
107627.m: The prothallus of a fern is tiny.

107628.q: Why do ferns need moisture to reproduce?
a: The male sex cells swim through water to the egg cell
The spores only sprout at the bottom of lakes
The fronds only flower in the rain
The roots need water for the seeds
107628.e: Egg cells and moving male sex cells form on the prothallus. The male cells swim through a thin film of water to the egg cell.
107628.m: Ferns need a film of water for fertilisation.

107630.q: What happens to the prothallus when the young fern plant has its own leaves and roots?
a: It turns woody and becomes a trunk
107630.e: The prothallus only supplies the young fern plant at the beginning. As soon as the fern is independent, the prothallus dies.
107630.m: The prothallus dies as soon as the young fern is independent.

107631.q: How does the prothallus of a fern feed itself?
a: It carries out photosynthesis with chlorophyll
It lives only on the spore's food reserves
107631.e: The prothallus is green and can make its own sugar using light. So it is a small independent plant.
107631.m: The fern prothallus feeds itself through photosynthesis.

a: A container in which spores form
A root hair that takes in water
A pore through which air flows
A store for starch in the trunk
